speaker: Maya
text: Last time: Cahokia, corn, and millions of people who'd never heard of Europe. This time: a Genoese sailor with bad math sails west looking for Asia. He finds a continent that wasn't lost, and gets its people's name wrong for five centuries. Three boxes: the Columbian Exchange, the encomienda system, the Treaty of Tordesillas. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Eight minutes, and they're yours.

speaker: Marcus
text: Start with the why. Europe's hungry for Asian spices and silk, and the old land routes run straight through Ottoman territory. After 1453, when Constantinople falls, those routes get more expensive and less reliable.

speaker: Maya
text: So the middleman gets greedy, and suddenly sailing into the unknown looks cheap by comparison.

speaker: Marcus
text: That's the gold motive. Then there's God: Spain's just finished the Reconquista, centuries of pushing Muslim rule out of Iberia that ended at Granada in 1492. Converting new souls feels like duty. And glory: Portugal's getting rich off the sea route to Asia, and no rival crown watches that quietly.

speaker: Maya
text: Gold, God, glory. Sounds like a pirate flag.

speaker: Marcus
text: Basically the Spanish business plan.

speaker: Maya
text: So Spain's rich and ready to spend?

speaker: Marcus
text: Opposite. The Reconquista was expensive. Spain's broke and distracted. What they've got is a navy, a grudge, and perfect timing.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay, Portugal first, then. How'd they crack the ocean?

speaker: Marcus
text: A prince who never sailed. Henry the Navigator bankrolls voyage after voyage down the African coast, and his captains get the tools that change everything: the caravel, a small fast ship built to maneuver; lateen sails, triangular ones that let a ship claw against the wind; and the astrolabe, which reads latitude off the stars, plus the magnetic compass for holding a course.

speaker: Maya
text: I capsized a kayak at camp when I was twelve and had to get towed in by a counselor. These guys crossed an ocean on a compass and a prayer.

speaker: Marcus
text: Sailors called the open Atlantic the sea of darkness. Every mile south was past the edge of every map they owned. 1488: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the southern tip of Africa. 1498: Vasco da Gama reaches India. Portugal owns the sea road to Asia, and Spain needs another way in.

speaker: Maya
text: In Civilization, Portugal's whole deal is trade routes. My brother plays them and just buys the map.

speaker: Marcus
text: Never played it. But your brother's strategy is historically accurate. Meanwhile Spain's got a Genoese sailor with a wild pitch: Niña, Pinta, Santa María.

speaker: Maya
text: I know those from a song in second grade. The tune's still in my head; the facts never made it.

speaker: Marcus
text: That'll do. Columbus figures Asia sits a few thousand miles west of the Canaries. The real number's more like ten thousand. He gets the shape of the earth right and the size of the trip wildly wrong.

speaker: Maya
text: So he fails upward into a continent.

speaker: Marcus
text: October 12, 1492, the Bahamas. He calls the people he meets Indians because he's sure he's reached Asia. He dies still insisting it. Four voyages — the Caribbean, the Venezuelan coast, Central America — and never the Asia he was chasing.

speaker: Maya
text: Five centuries of calling people by the wrong name has to be some kind of record.

speaker: Marcus
text: It's up there. Now Spain's holding islands, and Portugal's furious. They'd spent decades mapping that African route. Somebody had to split the difference.

speaker: Maya
text: The pope just drew a line?

speaker: Marcus
text: In 1494 Spain and Portugal sign the Treaty of Tordesillas. There's your first box: an imaginary line, 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands — a league's roughly three miles. West of the line: Spain. East: Portugal.

speaker: Maya
text: And France and England just agreed to that?

speaker: Marcus
text: They ignored it completely. But Spain and Portugal mostly honored it, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese today: the bulge of Brazil sticks out east of the line.

speaker: Maya
text: An imaginary line divvying up the planet, and it actually held? Okay.

speaker: Maya
text: Checking that one.

speaker: Marcus
text: After 1492, the traffic starts: crops, animals, people, and diseases, moving both directions across the Atlantic. In 1972 the historian Alfred Crosby gave it a name: the Columbian Exchange. Box two.

speaker: Maya
text: So that's the trade part: potatoes one way, sugar the other?

speaker: Marcus
text: Bigger than trade, and nobody signed anything. Maize, potatoes, and tomatoes sail east and help fuel population growth across Europe. Wheat and sugarcane sail west. Horses, cattle, and pigs sail west too. The Americas had never seen any of them.

speaker: Maya
text: And what about the diseases?

speaker: Marcus
text: Mostly west, and catastrophic. Smallpox, measles, influenza. In the hardest-hit places, eight or nine out of ten people die. The one that might've gone east is syphilis, and historians still argue about that one.

speaker: Maya
text: Box two, checked.

speaker: Marcus
text: So how do a few hundred Spaniards topple empires? Steel weapons and armor, horses, and above all disease. But no single one of those does it alone. It's the combination, plus alliances with Indigenous peoples who had their own reasons to fight the Aztecs.

speaker: Maya
text: So it wasn't the guns.

speaker: Marcus
text: Guns helped, but early guns were slow to reload and miserable in the rain. The real killers were invisible.

speaker: Maya
text: And then the encomienda. Box three.

speaker: Marcus
text: The crown grants a colonist the labor of a group of Native people. In exchange, the colonist owes them protection and Christianization. That's the deal on paper.

speaker: Maya
text: So it's slavery with paperwork?

speaker: Marcus
text: Close enough that historians argue about where the line is. Legally it wasn't chattel slavery. The crown insisted these were free subjects of the king. In practice, the work quotas were brutal and the protection was mostly theoretical.

speaker: Maya
text: Checking the last one. Protection in very large quotes.

speaker: Maya
text: Okay. That was a lot of ocean.

speaker: Maya
text: Three boxes, let's land them. Box one: the Treaty of Tordesillas. 1494, the pope's line, 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Spain gets the west, Portugal gets the east. Brazil ends up speaking Portuguese.

speaker: Marcus
text: Clean.

speaker: Maya
text: Box two: the Columbian Exchange. Crosby named it in 1972. Crops and animals and people and disease, moving both ways. Memory-check: in the hardest-hit places, eight or nine out of ten died — and that was mostly… east? No. West. Disease went west.

speaker: Marcus
text: West. Smallpox and measles sailed with the colonists.

speaker: Maya
text: Box three: encomienda — Spain's system for shipping labor across the Atlantic?

speaker: Marcus
text: Other direction. The labor was already there; that's the whole point. The crown granted a colonist Native labor, and the colonist owed protection and conversion back.

speaker: Maya
text: Right. And the protection part deserves the biggest air quotes in history.

speaker: Marcus
text: It does.

speaker: Maya
text: Two questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer out loud before I do. First, stimulus style: a Spanish priest in the 1550s writes that Native villages "stand empty, the fields untilled, for the sickness took the workers." What's the bigger pattern this source points to?

speaker: Maya
text: [5-second pause]

speaker: Maya
text: The Columbian Exchange's disease front — population collapse on a scale that broke Native communities and fed the demand for coerced labor. Second: in 1494, Spain and Portugal sign an agreement splitting new lands along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Name it, and explain Brazil.

speaker: Maya
text: [5-second pause]

speaker: Maya
text: The Treaty of Tordesillas. Brazil bulges east of the line, so it landed on Portugal's side. That's why it's the one country in South America that speaks Portuguese.

speaker: Maya
text: They sailed west looking for Asia — and found a world.

speaker: Marcus
text: Next time: England crashes the party: Drake, a vanished colony, and an Armada.

speaker: Maya
text: Check your three boxes.
